lessonTitle: Time Value of Money: Present Value, NPV and Equivalent Annual Cost

blocks.text: A plant engineer is offered 50 000 GBP of maintenance savings, but only at the end of five years, or a smaller sum today. Which is worth more? A pound received today can be invested or used to avoid a loan, so it is worth more than a pound promised later. Engineering economics turns that idea into numbers, so that a cash flow in year 5 can be compared fairly with one today.

blocks.markdown: The **time value of money** says that the worth of a cash flow depends on when it occurs. Cash today can earn a return or avoid interest, and future cash carries risk. We capture this with a **discount rate** $i$ (per year), which represents the minimum return the organisation requires on its capital. Throughout this unit cash flows occur at the **end of each year**, and the rate is constant and applied to costs in constant money, unless stated otherwise.

blocks.title: Present value (PV)
blocks.text: The value today of a cash flow $F$ that will occur $n$ years in the future, found by discounting it at rate $i$. A higher rate or a longer wait reduces the present value.

blocks.caption: Present value of a single future amount F received after n years at annual discount rate i.

blocks.title: Present value of one future saving
blocks.prompt: A maintenance contract will save 50 000 GBP in five years' time. Find its present value at a discount rate of 8% per year.

steps.text: Interpretation: 34 029 GBP invested now at 8% grows to 50 000 GBP in five years, so the two are equivalent for an organisation whose required return is 8%.

blocks.answer: The saving of 50 000 GBP in five years has a present value of about 34 030 GBP.

headers: PV of 100 000 GBP received in 10 years
blocks.caption: Effect of discount rate on a payment ten years away.

blocks.markdown: A project usually has a **stream** of cash flows: an outlay now (negative) and receipts or savings in later years. The **net present value (NPV)** discounts each flow to today and adds them. A positive NPV means the project earns more than the required return and adds value; a negative NPV means it earns less.

blocks.caption: C_t is the net cash flow at the end of year t (negative for outlays); t = 0 is today and is not discounted.

blocks.title: NPV of a machine investment
blocks.prompt: A machine costs 120 000 GBP now and gives net cash flows of 30 000, 40 000, 45 000, 45 000 and 40 000 GBP at the end of years 1 to 5. The discount rate is 10%. Find the NPV and say whether to accept the project.

steps.text: Sum of present values of inflows:
Decision rule: NPV is positive at the 10% required return, so the project is acceptable on financial grounds.

blocks.answer: NPV is about +29 700 GBP at 10%, so accept (subject to risk and non-financial factors).

blocks.title: NPV decision rule
blocks.text: Accept a project if its NPV is positive at the required discount rate; when choosing between mutually exclusive projects of equal life, choose the one with the higher NPV. Always state the discount rate and the cash-flow timing assumptions.

blocks.markdown: Comparing options is easier if a present amount is converted into an **equivalent annual cost (EAC)**, a level yearly amount over the project life, or vice versa. They are related by the **capital recovery factor** (CRF) and its inverse, the **present worth factor** of a uniform series.

blocks.caption: Conversion between a present worth PV and a level end-of-year annual amount A over n years at rate i.

blocks.title: Converting present worth to an annual cost
blocks.prompt: An 85 000 GBP pumping system has a life of 8 years and no salvage value. Express the capital cost as an equivalent annual cost at 6%.

steps.text: Check: eight payments of 13 688 GBP discounted at 6% sum to 85 000 GBP, so the conversion is reversible.

blocks.answer: The capital cost is equivalent to about 13 690 GBP per year over 8 years at 6%.

blocks.title: Common errors
blocks.text: Discounting the year-0 outlay; using a nominal rate with real (constant-money) cash flows; mixing months and years; and treating a high NPV as proof without testing how it changes if the discount rate or the cash flows are different.

points: Present value is a future amount divided by (1+i)^n; higher discount rates and longer delays reduce it.
Net present value adds the discounted cash flows, with the outlay at t = 0, and a positive NPV means the project earns more than the required return.
Present worth and equivalent annual cost are converted with the capital recovery factor, allowing options to be compared on a yearly basis.

questions.stem: A supplier will pay a rebate of 18 000 GBP in three years' time. At a discount rate of 7% per year, what is the present value of the rebate in GBP?
questions.explanation: The discount factor is 1.07^3 = 1.2250, so PV = 18 000/1.2250 = 14 693 GBP. The rebate is worth less than its face value today because the money could earn 7% per year in the meantime.

questions.stem: If the discount rate used to evaluate a project is increased, with all cash flows unchanged, what happens to the present value of a future saving?

distractorRationale.a: A higher rate discounts future amounts more heavily.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: PV = F/(1+i)^n falls as i rises.
distractorRationale.c: The rate appears in the denominator, so PV changes.
distractorRationale.d: Discounting does not change the sign of the cash flow.

questions.explanation: The denominator (1+i)^n grows as i increases, so the present value of every future amount falls. Distant cash flows are affected the most.

questions.stem: A tooling investment costs 40 000 GBP now and returns 15 000, 18 000 and 20 000 GBP at the end of years 1, 2 and 3. At a discount rate of 9%, calculate the net present value in GBP.
questions.explanation: The present values are 15 000/1.09 = 13 761, 18 000/1.09^2 = 15 150 and 20 000/1.09^3 = 15 444, totalling 44 355 GBP. Subtracting the 40 000 GBP outlay gives an NPV of about +4 355 GBP.

questions.stem: Two mutually exclusive projects of equal life are evaluated at the company's required return. Project X has an NPV of +12 000 GBP and Project Y has an NPV of +7 500 GBP. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Choose Y because it has the lower NPV and so lower risk
Choose X because it adds more value at the required return, other factors being equal
Choose neither because NPV must be zero
Choose the project with the shorter payback regardless of NPV

questions.correctOptionText: Choose X because it adds more value at the required return, other factors being equal

distractorRationale.a: A lower NPV is not lower risk; the NPV is the added value.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: the higher positive NPV adds more value for equal lives.
distractorRationale.c: A positive NPV means the project exceeds the required return.
distractorRationale.d: Payback ignores later flows and discounting.

questions.explanation: For mutually exclusive projects of equal life the higher NPV adds more value. Risk and non-financial factors should still be considered before the final choice.

questions.stem: A 64 000 GBP compressor has a life of 6 years and no salvage value. At 5% per year the capital recovery factor for 6 years is 0.19702. Calculate the equivalent annual cost of its purchase price in GBP per year.
questions.explanation: The equivalent annual cost is the present worth times the capital recovery factor: 64 000 x 0.19702 = 12 609 GBP per year. Running costs would be added to this figure when comparing machines.

questions.stem: A control upgrade will cut running costs by 4 200 GBP at the end of each year for 10 years. At 8% per year the present worth factor for a 10-year uniform series is 6.7101. What is the present worth of these savings in GBP?
questions.explanation: The present worth of a uniform series is the annual amount times the factor: 4 200 x 6.7101 = 28 182 GBP. If the upgrade costs less than this, it has a positive NPV at 8%.

questions.stem: A sum of money received today is worth more than the same sum promised in the future, because today's money can be invested to earn a return.
questions.explanation: This is the basis of discounting: money available now can earn interest or avoid borrowing costs. A future sum is therefore discounted to compare it with today's money.

questions.stem: A firm is choosing between two mutually exclusive 4-year projects at a required return of 10%. Project A costs 90 000 GBP and returns 30 000, 35 000, 40 000 and 30 000 GBP in years 1 to 4. Project B costs 60 000 GBP and returns 22 000, 26 000, 30 000 and 22 000 GBP in years 1 to 4. Calculate the NPV of each and recommend one, noting why a comparison on total cash returned could mislead.
markingGuide: Project A: discounted inflows 27 273 + 28 926 + 30 053 + 20 490 = 106 741 GBP; NPV = +16 741 GBP
Project B: discounted inflows 20 000 + 21 488 + 22 539 + 15 027 = 79 054 GBP; NPV = +19 054 GBP (about 19 050)
Recommends B because its NPV is higher, using equal lives
Notes that A returns more cash in total (135 000 against 100 000 GBP) but needs 30 000 GBP more capital
Total undiscounted cash ignores the time value of money and the size of the outlay
States assumptions (end-of-year flows, same rate, equal lives, no risk difference)
questions.explanation: The calculation must show discounting year by year. A strong answer explains that the higher total return of A does not outweigh the larger outlay and the later timing of its cash flows.

questions.stem: Explain what the discount rate represents and why a future cash flow is worth less than the same amount today. Illustrate with the present value of 100 000 GBP received in 10 years at 5% and at 12%, and comment on the effect of the rate on long-term projects.
markingGuide: The discount rate is the required return or opportunity cost of capital, reflecting investment alternatives and risk
Money today can be invested, so future sums are worth less
Higher rate lowers present value, especially for distant cash flows
Long-term projects with late benefits are very sensitive to the chosen rate, so sensitivity testing is needed
questions.explanation: Both numerical values must be correct and linked to the explanation. The key insight is that distant benefits are strongly penalised by high discount rates.

questions.stem: A water-treatment pump costs 150 000 GBP and lasts 12 years with no salvage value. Explain how to express its capital cost as an equivalent annual cost at 7% and why this is useful when comparing it with a cheaper pump that lasts only 7 years. Write the formula and state the assumptions.
markingGuide: Equivalent annual cost A = PV x CRF with CRF = i(1+i)^n/((1+i)^n - 1)
Applies i = 0.07 and n = 12 (CRF is about 0.1259, giving about 18 900 GBP per year)
Calculate the same for the cheaper pump with n = 7 and add running costs
Explains that this converts different lives to a common yearly basis
Assumptions: end-of-year cash flows, constant rate, replacement by an identical machine, no salvage
Notes that non-financial factors may also matter
questions.explanation: The marker accepts the formula with the correct factor and a clear explanation of why an annual basis allows fair comparison of unequal lives. The assumptions of the method must be stated.
